question_text: The angle between the plane of the ecliptic and the plane of equator is approximately :
explanation: The obliquity of the ecliptic, which represents the angle of tilt between the Earth's rotational equator and its orbital plane (the plane of the ecliptic), is approximately 23.5°.

question_text: Which is the highest latitude listed below at which the sun will rise above the horizon and set every day?
explanation: At the Arctic and Antarctic circles (~66.5°), the sun remains above or below the horizon for exactly 24 hours on the solstices. Thus, 66° is the highest latitude listed at which the sun will rise and set every single day of the year.

question_text: In which two months of the year is the difference between the transit of the Apparent Sun and Mean Sun across the Greenwich Meridian the greatest?
explanation: The Equation of Time describes the difference between Apparent Solar Time and Mean Solar Time. Due to the Earth's orbital eccentricity and axial tilt, this difference reaches its greatest values in February and November.

question_text: What is the highest latitude listed below at which the sun will reach an altitude of 90° above the horizon at some time during the year?
explanation: The sun can only reach the zenith (90° altitude directly overhead) at some point in the year within the tropical zone, which is bounded by the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn at approximately 23.5° latitude.

question_text: Assuming mid-latitudes (40° to 50°N/S).At which time of year is the relationship between the length of day and night, as well as the rate of change of declination of the sun, changing at the greatest rate?
explanation: At the spring and autumn equinoxes, the sun crosses the Earth's equatorial plane, causing the solar declination and the relative length of day and night to change at their maximum rate.

question_text: At what approximate date is the earth closest to the sun (perihelion)?
explanation: The Earth is closest to the sun in its elliptical orbit at perihelion, which occurs annually in the beginning of January when the Earth is approximately 147 million kilometers away.

question_text: At what approximate date is the earth furthest from the sun (aphelion)?
explanation: The Earth is furthest from the sun at aphelion, which occurs annually in the beginning of July when the Earth is approximately 152 million kilometers away from the sun.

question_text: Seasons are due to the:
option_a: inclination of the polar axis with the ecliptic plane
option_b: Earth's elliptical orbit around the Sun
option_c: Earth's rotation on its polar axis
option_d: variable distance between Earth and Sun
explanation: Seasons are caused by the tilt of the Earth's rotational axis (polar axis) relative to the perpendicular of its orbital plane (the ecliptic plane) as it orbits the sun.

question_text: An aircraft departs from position A (04°10' S 178°22'W) and flies northward following the meridian for 2950 NM. It then flies westward along the parallel of latitude for 382 NM to position B. The coordinates of position B are?
explanation: Flying north for 2950 NM along the meridian corresponds to a change of 49°10' in latitude, moving from 04°10'S to 45°00'N. Flying west along the parallel of 45°N for 382 NM represents a change in longitude of 382 / cos(45°) = 540.2 minutes (9°00'W), which yields a final position of 45°00'N 172°38'E.

question_text: The angle between the true great-circle track and the true rhumb-line track joining the following points: A (60° S 165° W) B (60° S 177° E), at the place of departure A, is:
explanation: The angle between the great circle and rhumb line tracks at the point of departure is the conversion angle: 0.5 * dlong * sin(mean lat). For points A and B, dlong is 18° and mean latitude is 60°S, yielding 0.5 * 18 * sin(60°) = 7.8°.

question_text: Given: Waypoint 1. 60°S 030°W Waypoint 2. 60°S 020°WWhat will be the approximate latitude shown on the display unit of an inertial navigation system at longitude 025°W?
explanation: On a great circle track between two points on the same parallel of latitude in the Southern Hemisphere, the path curves toward the south pole. Consequently, at the midpoint longitude (25°W), the latitude is slightly south of 60°S, measuring 60°06'S.

question_text: What is the time required to travel along the parallel of latitude 60° N between meridians 010° E and 030° W at a groundspeed of 480 kt?
explanation: A degree of longitude along the 60°N parallel equals 60 * cos(60°) = 30 NM. The distance between 10°E and 30°W (40° dlong) is 40 * 30 = 1200 NM. At a groundspeed of 480 kt, the travel time is 1200 / 480 = 2.5 hours, or 2 hours 30 minutes.

question_text: A Rhumb line is :
option_a: a line on the surface of the earth cutting all meridians at the same angle
option_b: the shortest distance between two points on a Polyconic projection
option_c: any straight line on a Lambert projection
option_d: a line convex to the nearest pole on a Mercator projection
explanation: By definition, a rhumb line (or loxodromic curve) is a line on the surface of the Earth that crosses all meridians of longitude at the same constant angle.

question_text: A great circle track joins position A (59°S 141°W) and B (61°S 148°W). What is the difference between the great circle track at A and B?
explanation: The difference between the great circle track at the departure and destination points is the Earth convergency, calculated as dlong * sin(mean lat). With a dlong of 7° and mean latitude of 60°S, the track increases by approximately 6°.

question_text: What is the longitude of a position 6 NM to the east of 58°42'N 094°00'W?
explanation: Departure along a parallel is calculated as dlong = Departure / cos(latitude). For a 6 NM eastward displacement at 58°42'N, the change in longitude is 6 / cos(58.7°) = 11.55 minutes, resulting in a new longitude of 093°48.5'W.

question_text: Given: value for the ellipticity of the Earth is 1/297. Earth's semi-major axis, as measured at the equator, equals 6378.4 km. What is the semi-minor axis (km) of the earth at the axis of the Poles?
explanation: The ellipticity of the Earth is defined as (a - b) / a, where a is the semi-major axis (6378.4 km) and b is the semi-minor axis. Solving for b yields 6378.4 * (1 - 1/297) = 6356.9 km.

question_text: Position A is located on the equator at longitude 130°00E. Position B is located 100 NM from A on a bearing of 225°(T).The coordinates of position B are:
explanation: Flying 100 NM on a bearing of 225° from the equator at 130°E gives a dlat of 100 * cos(225°) = 70.7 NM south (1°11'S) and departure of 70.7 NM west. The dlong is 70.7 / cos(0.59°) = 70.7 minutes (1°11'W), yielding coordinates of 01°11'S 128°49'E.

question_text: In order to fly from position A (10°00'N, 030°00'W) to position B (30°00'N, 050°00'W), maintaining a constant true course, it is necessary to fly:
option_d: a straight line plotted on a Lambert chart
explanation: A rhumb line track represents a path of constant heading (constant true course) between two geographical coordinates on the Earth's surface.

question_text: The rhumb line track between position A (45°00'N, 010°00'W) and position B (48°30'N, 015°00'W) is approximately:
explanation: Using the rhumb line formula: track = arctan(departure / dlat), where dlat is 210 NM north and departure is 205.5 NM west. The track is approximately 44° west of north, which translates to a true course of 315°.

question_text: The diameter of the Earth is approximately:
explanation: Based on geodetic measurements, the mean diameter of the Earth is approximately 12,700 kilometers, with a slightly larger equatorial diameter than polar diameter.

question_text: The maximum difference between geocentric and geodetic latitude occurs at about:
explanation: The oblateness of the Earth causes a difference between geocentric latitude (measured from the center) and geodetic latitude (measured from the surface normal), which reaches its maximum value of 11.6 minutes at 45° latitude.

question_text: The great circle distance between position A (59°34.1'N 008°08.4'E) and B (30°25.9'N 171°51.6'W) is:
explanation: Since the coordinates are exactly 180° apart in longitude, the great circle route passes directly over the pole. The distance is the sum of the colatitudes: (90° - 59°34.1') + (90° - 30°25.9') = 90° of arc, which equals 5400 NM.

question_text: Given:Position A 45°N, ?°EPosition B 45°N, 45°15'EDistance A-B = 280 NMB is to the East of ARequired: longitude of position A?
explanation: At 45°N, a departure of 280 NM corresponds to a change in longitude of 280 / cos(45°) = 396 minutes (6°36'). Since B is east of A, the longitude of A is 45°15'E - 6°36' = 38°39'E.

question_text: If an aeroplane was to circle around the Earth following parallel 60°N at a ground speed of 480 kt. In order to circle around the Earth along the equator in the same amount of time, it should fly at a ground speed of:
explanation: The radius of the parallel of latitude at 60°N is exactly half of the Earth's equatorial radius (cos(60°) = 0.5). To fly around the equator in the same time as circling the 60°N parallel at 480 kt, the aircraft must fly twice as fast, which is 960 kt.

question_text: An aircraft passes position A (60°00'N 120°00'W) on route to position B (60°00'N 140°30'W). What is the great circle track on departure from A?
explanation: The initial great circle track is found by adding the conversion angle to the rhumb line track of 270°. With a dlong of 20.5° at 60°N, the conversion angle is 0.5 * 20.5 * sin(60°) = 8.9°, resulting in an initial track of 279°.

question_text: An aeroplane flies from A (59°S 142°W) to B (61°S 148°W) with a TAS of 480 kt. The autopilot is engaged and coupled with an Inertial Navigation System in which AB track is active.On route AB, the true track:
explanation: The change in track angle along a great circle route is determined by the Earth convergency: dlong * sin(mean lat). For a route from 142°W to 148°W (dlong = 6°) at a mean latitude of 60°S, the true track increases by 5°.

question_text: The circumference of the earth is approximately:
explanation: The circumference of the Earth along a great circle represents 360 degrees of arc, which corresponds exactly to 360 * 60 NM/degree = 21,600 Nautical Miles.

question_text: The Great Circle bearing of 'B' (70°S 060°E), from 'A' (70° S 030° W), is approximately:
explanation: Plotting the great circle route between two points at 70°S shows a path that curves toward the south pole. The initial great circle bearing from 30°W to 60°E is approximately 135°(T).

question_text: At what approximate latitude is the length of one minute of arc along a meridian equal to one NM (1852 m) correct?
explanation: Because of the Earth's oblate spheroid shape, the curvature varies with latitude. The length of one minute of arc along a meridian corresponds exactly to one standard international nautical mile (1852 meters) at 45° latitude.

question_text: An aircraft flies a great circle track from 56° N 070° W to 62° N 110° E. The total distance travelled is?
explanation: Guam and Los Angeles longitudes are exactly 180° apart, meaning the great circle route passes over the pole. The total distance is the sum of colatitudes: (90 - 56) + (90 - 62) = 62 degrees of arc, which equals 3,720 NM.

question_text: Given :A is N55° 000°B is N54° E010°The average true course of the great circle is 100°.The true course of the rhumbline at point A is:
explanation: For a great circle track between two coordinates, the track angle changes continuously along the route. The midpoint true track of the great circle equals the constant track of the rhumb line, which is 100°.

question_text: The circumference of the parallel of latitude at 60°N is approximately:
explanation: The circumference of a parallel of latitude is calculated as the equatorial circumference multiplied by the cosine of the latitude. At 60°N, this equals 21,600 * cos(60°) = 10,800 NM.

question_text: Given:The coordinates of the heliport at Issy les Moulineaux are:N48°50' E002°16.5'The coordinates of the antipodes are :
explanation: The antipodal point of any geographical coordinate is located at the opposite latitude (S48°50') and a longitude that is 180° away from the starting meridian (180° - 2°16.5'E = 177°43.5'W).

question_text: Given:Position 'A' is N00° E100°, Position 'B' is 240°(T), 200 NM from 'A'.What is the position of 'B'?
explanation: A track of 240° for 200 NM from the equator at 100°E gives a dlat of 200 * cos(240°) = 100 NM south (1°40'S). The departure is 200 * sin(240°) = -173.2 NM west, which at 0°50'S mean latitude yields a dlong of 173.2 / cos(0.83°) = 173.2 minutes (2°53'W), giving a position of S01°40' E097°07'.

question_text: The duration of civil twilight is the time:
option_a: between sunset and when the centre of the sun is 6° below the true horizon
option_b: agreed by the international aeronautical authorities which is 12 minutes
option_c: needed by the sun to move from the apparent height of 0° to the apparent height of 6°
option_d: between sunset and when the centre of the sun is 12° below the true horizon
explanation: By international astronomical definition, the duration of civil twilight is the time interval between sunset (or sunrise) and when the center of the sun's disk is exactly 6° below the true horizon.

question_text: On the 27th of February, at 52°S and 040°E, the sunrise is at 0243 UTC. On the same day, at 52°S and 035°W, the sunrise is at:
explanation: Sunrise occurs at the same Local Mean Time (LMT) for any points at the same latitude on the same day. Since 35°W is 75° longitude west of 40°E (a difference of 5 hours), sunrise occurs 5 hours later in UTC, at 0743 UTC.

question_text: What is the local mean time, position 65°25'N 123°45'W at 2200 UTC?
explanation: To find the Local Mean Time (LMT) from UTC, apply the longitude correction of 4 minutes per degree. For 123°45'W, the correction is 8 hours 15 minutes behind UTC, yielding an LMT of 1345 when UTC is 2200.

question_text: The Local Mean Time at longitude 095°20'W, at 0000 UTC, is :
explanation: Apply the longitude correction of 4 minutes per degree to find the Local Mean Time. For 095°20'W, the time is 6 hours 21 minutes 20 seconds behind UTC, resulting in an LMT of 17:38:40 on the previous day.

question_text: 5 HR 20 MIN 20 SEC corresponds to a longitude difference of:
explanation: To convert a time difference into a longitude difference, use the rate of 15° of longitude per hour (or 1° per 4 minutes). A duration of 5h 20m 20s converts to 75° (5h) + 5° (20m) + 5' (20s) = 80°05'.

question_text: (For this question use annex 061-2304A)The UTC of sunrise on 6 December at WINNIPEG (Canada) (49°50'N 097°30'W) is:
explanation: Using the sunrise tables in the annex for 6 December at latitude 49°50'N, find the local time of sunrise. Applying the longitude correction for Winnipeg (097°30'W) converts the local time to 1413 UTC.

question_text: (For this question use annexes 061-2305A and 061-2305B) When it is 1000 Standard Time in Kuwait, the Standard Time in Algeria is:
explanation: Kuwait operates on UTC+3 while Algeria operates on UTC+1. Therefore, when it is 1000 Standard Time in Kuwait, the Standard Time in Algeria (which is 2 hours behind) is 0800.

question_text: (For this question use annex 061-2325A to 061-2325D)An aircraft takes off from Guam at 2300 Standard Time on 30 April local date. After a flight of 11 HR 15 MIN it lands at Los Angeles (California). What is the Standard Time and local date of arrival (assume summer time rules apply)?
explanation: Guam (UTC+10) to Los Angeles (UTC-7 summer time) has a time difference of 17 hours. Departing Guam at 2300 standard time on 30 April local date and flying for 11h 15m gives an arrival time of 1715 on 30 April in Los Angeles.

question_text: (For this question use annex 061-2326A to 061-2326D)When it is 0600 Standard Time in Queensland (Australia) the Standard Time in Hawaii (USA) is:
explanation: Queensland standard time is UTC+10, and Hawaii standard time is UTC-10, making Hawaii 20 hours behind Queensland. When it is 0600 Standard Time in Queensland, the Standard Time in Hawaii is 1000 on the previous day.

question_text: The main reason that day and night, throughout the year, have different duration, is due to the:
option_a: inclination of the ecliptic to the equator
option_c: relative speed of the sun along the ecliptic
option_d: gravitational effect of the sun and moon on the speed of rotation of the earth
explanation: The primary cause of the varying duration of day and night throughout the year is the inclination (tilt) of the Earth's equator relative to the plane of the ecliptic (its orbit around the sun).

question_text: What is the meaning of the term ""standard time"" ?
option_a: It is the time set by the legal authorities for a country or part of a country
option_b: It is the time zone system applicable only in the USA
option_c: It is an expression for local mean time
option_d: It is another term for UTC
explanation: Standard Time is the legally authorized time zone system established by local authorities for a specific country or region, typically defined in whole-hour offsets from UTC.

question_text: Civil twilight is defined by :
option_a: sun altitude is 6° below the celestial horizon
option_b: sun altitude is 12° below the celestial horizon
option_c: sun altitude is 18° below the celestial horizon
option_d: sun upper edge tangential to horizon
explanation: Civil twilight is officially defined as the period of time when the center of the sun is between 0° and 6° below the celestial horizon.

question_text: Given: true track is 348°, drift 17° left, variation 32° W, deviation 4°E. What is the compass heading?
explanation: True Heading is True Track plus/minus drift (drift left requires adding drift to find heading: 348° + 17° = 005° TH). Magnetic Heading is True Heading plus variation west (005° + 32° = 037° MH). Compass Heading is Magnetic Heading minus deviation east (037° - 4° = 033° CH).

question_text: An Agonic line is a line that connects:
option_b: positions that have the same variation
option_d: points of equal magnetic horizontal field strength
explanation: An agonic line is a line drawn on an aeronautical chart that connects all geographic locations where the magnetic variation is exactly 0°.

question_text: Isogonic lines connect positions that have:
option_d: the same angle of magnetic dip
explanation: An isogonic line (or isogonal) is a line on a map or chart that connects geographic points sharing the same magnetic variation.

question_text: Compass deviation is defined as the angle between:
option_d: the horizontal and the total intensity of the earth's magnetic field
explanation: Compass deviation is defined as the angular difference between Magnetic North (as indicated by a compass free of local magnetic fields) and Compass North (as indicated by the aircraft's compass).

question_text: The angle between True North and Magnetic North is called :
explanation: Magnetic variation (or magnetic declination) is defined as the horizontal angle between the direction of True North (the geographic meridian) and Magnetic North.

question_text: Deviation applied to magnetic heading gives:
explanation: Applying the compass deviation correction to a Magnetic Heading yields the Compass Heading, which is the reading displayed on the aircraft's magnetic compass.

question_text: Isogrives are lines that connect positions that have:
option_b: the same horizontal magnetic field strength
explanation: Isogrives are lines drawn on a grid navigation chart that connect geographic points of equal grivation (the angular difference between Grid North and Magnetic North).

question_text: The lines on the earth's surface that join points of equal magnetic variation are called:
explanation: Isogonals (or isogonic lines) are lines on a map or chart that connect points of equal magnetic variation (declination).

question_text: A negative (westerly) magnetic variation signifies that :
option_a: True North is East of Magnetic North
option_b: True North is West of Magnetic North
option_c: Compass North is East of Magnetic North
option_d: Compass North is West of Magnetic North
explanation: A negative or westerly magnetic variation means that Magnetic North lies to the west of True North. Consequently, True North is situated to the east of Magnetic North.

question_text: The angle between Magnetic North and Compass North is called:
explanation: Compass deviation is defined as the angular difference between Magnetic North (free of local aircraft fields) and Compass North (as indicated by the cockpit compass).

question_text: The north and south magnetic poles are the only positions on the earth's surface where:
option_a: a freely suspended compass needle will stand vertical
option_c: a freely suspended compass needle will stand horizontal
option_d: the value of magnetic variation equals 90°
explanation: At the magnetic poles, the Earth's magnetic field lines are completely vertical. Therefore, a freely suspended magnetic needle will stand vertically (90° dip) at these locations.

question_text: The rhumb-line distance between points A (60°00'N 002°30'E) and B (60°00'N 007°30'W) is:
explanation: The rhumb line distance along a parallel of latitude is calculated as: Distance = dlong (in minutes) * cos(latitude). For a 10° longitude difference (600 minutes) at 60°N, the distance is 600 * cos(60°) = 300 NM.

question_text: An aircraft flies the following rhumb line tracks and distances from position 04°00'N 030°00'W :600 NM South, then 600 NM East, then 600 NM North, then 600 NM West.The final position of the aircraft is:
explanation: Flying 600 NM south along the meridian from 04°N 30°W reaches 06°S. Flying 600 NM east at 06°S gives a dlong of 600 / cos(6°S) = 603.3' (10°03'E). After flying 600 NM north back to 04°N, flying 600 NM west at 04°N gives a dlong of 600 / cos(4°N) = 601.5' (10°01.5'W), resulting in a final longitude of 30°W - 10°03'E + 10°01.5'W = 29°58.5'W (rounds to 29°58'W).

question_text: What is the final position after the following rhumb line tracks and distances have been followed from position 60°00'N 030°00'W?South for 3600 NM, East for 3600 NM, North for 3600 NM, West for 3600 NM.The final position of the aircraft is:
explanation: Flying 3600 NM south from 60°N 30°W reaches the equator (00°N/S). Flying 3600 NM east along the equator represents a dlong of 3600 minutes (60°E), reaching 30°E. Flying 3600 NM north reaches 60°N. Flying 3600 NM west along 60°N represents a dlong of 3600 / cos(60°) = 7200 minutes (120°W), giving a final longitude of 30°E - 120°W = 090°00'W.

question_text: An aircraft departing A(N40º 00´ E080º 00´) flies a constant true track of 270º at a ground speed of 120 kt. What are the coordinates of the position reached in 6 HR?
explanation: Flying westward along the parallel of 40°N at 120 kt for 6 hours covers a distance of 720 NM. The change in longitude (dlong) is calculated as: dlong = Distance / cos(latitude) = 720 / cos(40°) = 940 minutes (15°40'W), which subtracted from 080°00'E yields 064°20'E.

question_text: A flight is to be made from 'A' 49°S 180°E/W to 'B' 58°S, 180°E/W.The distance in kilometres from 'A' to 'B' is approximately:
explanation: The distance in latitude between 49°S and 58°S along the 180° meridian is 9 degrees of arc. Since 1 degree of latitude equals 60 NM, the distance is 9 * 60 = 540 NM. Converting to kilometers: 540 * 1.852 = 1,000 km.

question_text: An aircraft at position 60°N 005°W tracks 090°(T) for 315 km.On completion of the flight the longitude will be:
explanation: Distance = 315 km / 1.852 = 170.1 NM. The change in longitude (dlong) along the parallel of 60°N is: dlong = Distance / cos(latitude) = 170.1 / cos(60°) = 340.2 minutes (5°40'E). Starting at 005°00'W and tracking east yields a final longitude of 000°40'E.

question_text: The 'departure' between positions 60°N 160°E and 60°N 'x' is 900 NM.What is the longitude of 'x'?
explanation: The change in longitude (dlong) is calculated from the departure distance using the formula: dlong = Departure / cos(latitude). For a departure of 900 NM at 60°N, dlong = 900 / cos(60°) = 1800 minutes (30°). Flying east from 160°E reaches a final longitude of 170°W.

question_text: An aircraft at latitude 02°20'N tracks 180°(T) for 685 km.On completion of the flight the latitude will be:
explanation: A distance of 685 km is equivalent to 685 / 1.852 = 370 NM. Since 1 NM along a meridian equals 1 minute of latitude, flying due south (track 180°) for 370 NM represents a change of 6°10' in latitude. Subtracting this from 02°20'N yields a final latitude of 03°50'S.

question_text: An aircraft at latitude 10° South flies north at a GS of 890 km/HR. What will its latitude be after 1.5 HR?
explanation: Distance covered in 1.5 hours at a groundspeed of 890 km/h is 1335 km, which equals 1335 / 1.852 = 720.8 NM. Since 1 NM equals 1 minute of latitude along a meridian, flying due north for 720.8 minutes represents a latitude change of 12°01'N. Starting at 10°S, the final latitude is 02°00'N.

question_text: An aircraft at latitude 10°North flies south at a groundspeed of 445 km/HR.What will be its latitude after 3 HR?
explanation: Distance covered in 3 hours at a groundspeed of 445 km/h is 1335 km, which equals 1335 / 1.852 = 720.8 NM. Flying due south along a meridian for 720.8 NM represents a change in latitude of 12°01'S, which starting from 10°N yields a final latitude of 02°00'S.

question_text: Given : Position 'A' N60 W020,Position 'B' N60 W021, Position 'C' N59 W020. What are, respectively, the distances from A to B and from A to C?
explanation: The distance from A to B along the parallel of 60°N is calculated as: Distance = dlong (1° = 60 minutes) * cos(60°) = 30 NM. The distance from A to C along the meridian of 20°W is the change in latitude: N60 to N59 is 1° of latitude, which equals 60 NM.

question_text: An aircraft is over position HO (55°30'N 060°15'W), where YYR VOR (53°30'N 060°15'W) can be received. The magnetic variation is 31°W at HO and 28°W at YYR.What is the radial from YYR?
explanation: The radial from a VOR is the magnetic bearing FROM the station, which is calculated using the magnetic variation at the VOR station itself. Since the aircraft is directly north of the VOR, the true bearing from the VOR is 360°. Applying the 28°W variation at YYR: Magnetic Radial = 360° + 28° = 028°.

question_text: When is the magnetic compass most effective?
option_a: About midway between the magnetic poles
option_b: In the region of the magnetic South Pole.
option_c: In the region of the magnetic North Pole.
explanation: A direct reading magnetic compass relies on the horizontal component (H) of the Earth's magnetic field to align itself. This horizontal component is strongest midway between the magnetic poles (at the magnetic equator) and becomes zero at the poles, making the compass most effective there.

question_text: What is the value of the magnetic dip at the magnetic south pole ?
explanation: At the magnetic South Pole, the Earth's magnetic flux lines enter the surface vertically. Therefore, the magnetic dip (the angle between the magnetic vector and the horizontal plane) is exactly 90°.

question_text: The value of magnetic variation:
option_b: must be 0° at the magnetic equator
option_c: varies between a maximum of 45° East and 45° West
explanation: Magnetic variation represents the horizontal angle between True North and Magnetic North. Depending on location, it can range anywhere from 0° up to a maximum value of 180° East or West.

question_text: Isogonals converge at the:
option_a: North and South geographic and magnetic poles
option_d: North and South magnetic poles only
explanation: Isogonals are lines of equal variation that connect the geographic poles (where all true meridians meet) and the magnetic poles (where all magnetic meridians meet), causing them to converge at both sets of poles.

question_text: A line drawn on a chart which joins all points where the value of magnetic variation is zero is called an:
explanation: An agonic line is a specific isogonal that connects all geographic locations on the Earth's surface where the magnetic variation is exactly 0°.

question_text: The horizontal component of the earth's magnetic field:
option_a: is approximately the same at magnetic latitudes 50°N and 50°S
option_b: weakens with increasing distance from the magnetic poles
option_c: weakens with increasing distance from the nearer magnetic pole
option_d: is approximately the same at all magnetic latitudes less than 60°
explanation: Because of the Earth's dipolar magnetic field structure, the horizontal component (H) is symmetrical about the magnetic equator. Consequently, the horizontal field strength is approximately equal at corresponding magnetic latitudes of 50°N and 50°S.

question_text: Complete the following statement regarding magnetic variation. The charted values of magnetic variation on earth normally change annually due to:
option_a: magnetic pole movement causing numerical values at all locations to increase or decrease
option_b: magnetic pole movement causing numerical values at all locations to increase.
option_c: a reducing field strength causing numerical values at all locations to decrease.
option_d: an increasing field strength causing numerical values at all locations to increase.
explanation: The Earth's magnetic field is not static; the magnetic poles undergo continuous slow movement over time. This movement causes the local values of magnetic variation to slowly increase or decrease annually at any given location.

question_text: The Earth can be considered as being a magnet with the:
option_a: blue pole near the north pole of the earth and the direction of the magnetic force pointing straight down to the earth's surface
option_b: red pole near the north pole of the earth and the direction of the magnetic force pointing straight down to the earth's surface
option_c: blue pole near the north pole of the earth and the direction of the magnetic force pointing straight up from the earth's surface
option_d: red pole near the north pole of the earth and the direction of the magnetic force pointing straight up from the earth's surface
explanation: By physical convention, the magnetic pole located in the Northern Hemisphere attracts the north-seeking (red) pole of a compass. This means it is physically a magnetic South or 'blue' pole, and the magnetic field lines point vertically downward into the Earth's surface there.

question_text: Which of the following statements concerning earth magnetism is completely correct?
option_a: An isogonal is a line which connects places with the same magnetic variation, the aclinic is the line of zero magnetic dip
option_b: An isogonal is a line which connects places with the same magnetic variation, the agonic line is the line of zero magnetic dip
option_c: An isogonal is a line which connects places of equal dip, the aclinic is the line of zero magnetic dip
option_d: An isogonal is a line which connects places with the same magnetic variation, the aclinic connects places with the same magnetic field strength
explanation: An isogonal is defined as a line joining places of equal magnetic variation. The aclinic line is the magnetic equator, which connects all points of zero magnetic dip (where a compass needle stays perfectly horizontal).

question_text: Which of the following statements concerning the earth's magnetic field is completely correct?
option_a: The blue pole of the earth's magnetic field is situated in North Canada
option_b: At the earth's magnetic equator, the inclination varies depending on whether the geograhic equator is north or south of the magnetic equator
option_c: The earth's magnetic field can be classified as transient, semi-permanent or permanent
option_d: Dip is the angle between total magnetic field and vertical field component
explanation: The magnetic North Pole in northern Canada acts as the magnetic 'South' (blue) pole of the Earth's magnetic dipole, attracting the north-seeking end of a compass needle.

question_text: The sensitivity of a direct reading compass varies:
option_a: directly with the horizontal component of the earth's magnetic field
option_b: directly with the vertical component of the earth's magnetic field
option_c: inversely with both vertical and horizontal components of the earth's magnetic field
option_d: inversely with the vertical component of the earth's magnetic field
explanation: The directive force that aligns a direct-reading compass is the horizontal component (H) of the Earth's magnetic field. Compass sensitivity is directly proportional to H, which is strongest at the magnetic equator and zero at the magnetic poles.

question_text: Isogonals are lines of equal :
explanation: By definition, isogonals are lines drawn on maps or charts that connect points sharing the same value of magnetic variation.

question_text: At a specific location, the value of magnetic variation:
option_b: depends on the type of compass installed
explanation: Due to the fluid nature of the Earth's outer core, the magnetic field undergoes secular changes. This causes the value of magnetic variation at any specific geographic location to change slowly over time.

question_text: When an aircraft on a westerly heading on the northern hemisphere accelerates, the effect of the acceleration error causes the magnetic compass to:
option_a: indicate a turn towards the north
option_b: lag behind the turning rate of the aircraft
option_c: indicate a turn towards the south
option_d: to turn faster than the actual turning rate of the aircraft
explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere, acceleration on a westerly heading tilts the compass card due to inertia acting on the compass's pendulous offset. This tilt allows the vertical component of the Earth's field to rotate the compass, causing a false turn indication toward the north.

question_text: When decelerating on a westerly heading in the Northern hemisphere, the compass card of a direct reading magnetic compass will turn :
option_a: clockwise giving an apparent turn toward the south
option_b: anti-clockwise giving an apparent turn towards the south
option_c: clockwise giving an apparent turn towards the north
option_d: anti-clockwise giving an apparent turn towards the north
explanation: Deceleration on a westerly heading in the Northern Hemisphere causes the compass card to tilt, allowing the vertical component of the Earth's magnetic field to rotate the compass. This rotation appears as a clockwise card movement, indicating an apparent turn toward the south.

question_text: An aircraft in the northern hemisphere makes an accurate rate one turn to the right/starboard. If the initial heading was 330°, after 30 seconds of the turn the direct reading magnetic compass should read:
option_d: more or less than 060° depending on the pendulous suspension used
explanation: When turning through North in the Northern Hemisphere, the vertical component of the Earth's magnetic field tilts the compass card, causing it to rotate in the same direction as the turn. This creates a lag effect, meaning the compass under-indicates the turn and reads less than the actual heading (less than 060° after a 90° turn).

question_text: When turning right from 330°(C) to 040°(C) in the northern hemisphere, the reading of a direct reading magnetic compass will:
option_a: under-indicate the turn and liquid swirl will increase the effect
option_b: over-indicate the turn and liquid swirl will decrease the effect
option_c: under-indicate the turn and liquid swirl will decrease the effect
option_d: over-indicate the turn and liquid swirl will increase the effect
explanation: When turning right through North in the Northern Hemisphere, the vertical magnetic component tilts the compass card, causing it to lag (under-indicate) the turn. Viscous drag of the compass fluid (liquid swirl) acts in the direction of the turn, which further rotates the card and increases this under-indication.

question_text: When accelerating on an easterly heading in the Northern hemisphere, the compass card of a direct reading magnetic compass will turn :
option_a: clockwise giving an apparent turn toward the north
option_b: clockwise giving an apparent turn toward the south
option_c: anti-clockwise giving an apparent turn toward the north
option_d: anti-clockwise giving an apparent turn toward the south
explanation: Acceleration on an easterly heading in the Northern Hemisphere causes the compass card to tilt due to inertia. The vertical component of the Earth's field then acts on the tilted card, rotating it clockwise to produce a false turn indication toward the north.

question_text: An aircraft in the northern hemisphere is making an accurate rate one turn to the right. If the initial heading was 135°, after 30 seconds the direct reading magnetic compass should read:
option_d: more or less than 225° depending on the pendulous suspension used
explanation: When turning through South in the Northern Hemisphere, the compass card tilts in a way that causes the vertical magnetic component to rotate the card in the opposite direction of the turn. This creates a lead effect, causing the compass to over-indicate the turn and read more than the actual heading (more than 225° after a 90° turn).

question_text: When accelerating on a westerly heading in the northern hemisphere, the compass card of a direct reading magnetic compass will turn:
option_a: anti-clockwise giving an apparent turn towards the north
option_b: anti-clockwise giving an apparent turn towards the south
option_c: clockwise giving an apparent turn towards the north
option_d: clockwise giving an apparent turn towards the south
explanation: Acceleration on a westerly heading in the Northern Hemisphere causes the compass card to tilt due to inertia. This tilt allows the vertical magnetic component to rotate the card anti-clockwise, producing a false turn indication toward the north.

question_text: Which of the following statements is correct concerning the effect of turning errors on a direct reading compass?
option_a: Turning errors are greatest on north/south headings, and are greatest at high latitudes
option_b: Turning errors are greatest on east/west headings, and are least at high latitudes
option_c: Turning errors are greatest on north/south headings, and are least at high latitudes
option_d: Turning errors are greatest on east/west headings, and are greatest at high latitudes
explanation: Turning errors on a direct-reading compass are caused by the vertical component of the Earth's magnetic field (Z) acting on a tilted compass card. Because Z is strongest at high latitudes and card tilt is maximized on North/South headings, turning errors are greatest under these conditions.

question_text: At the magnetic equator, when accelerating after take off on heading West, a direct reading compass :
option_d: indicates a turn to the south
explanation: At the magnetic equator, the Earth's magnetic field is entirely horizontal, and the vertical component (Z) is zero. Because there is no vertical component to act on a tilted card, acceleration errors do not occur, and the compass indicates the correct heading.

question_text: Permanent magnetism in aircraft arises chiefly from:
option_a: hammering, and the effect of the earth's magnetic field, whilst under construction
option_b: exposure to the earth's magnetic field during normal operation
option_c: the combined effect of aircraft electrical equipment and the earth's magnetic field
option_d: the effect of internal wiring and exposure to electrical storms
explanation: Permanent magnetism in an aircraft's structure is primarily induced during construction. The process of hammering and riveting ferrous metals in the presence of the Earth's magnetic field aligns the magnetic domains, creating a permanent magnetic field.

question_text: Concerning direct reading magnetic compasses, in the northern hemisphere, it can be said that :
option_a: on an Easterly heading, a longitudinal acceleration causes an apparent turn to the North
option_b: on an Easterly heading, a longitudinal acceleration causes an apparent turn to the South
option_c: on a Westerly heading, a longitudinal acceleration causes an apparent turn to the South
option_d: on a Westerly heading, a longitudinal deceleration causes an apparent turn to the North
explanation: According to the ANDS rule (Accelerate North, Decelerate South), longitudinal acceleration on an Easterly heading in the Northern Hemisphere causes the compass card to rotate, indicating a false turn toward the north.

question_text: In northern hemisphere, during an acceleration in an easterly direction, the magnetic compass will indicate:
option_c: an apparent turn to the South
explanation: Acceleration on an easterly heading in the Northern Hemisphere causes an apparent turn toward the North. A false turn to the north from an easterly heading (090°) results in a decrease in the indicated heading (e.g., towards 080°).

question_text: The purpose of compass check swing is to:
option_a: measure the angle between Magnetic North and Compass North
option_b: cancel out the vertical component of the earth's magnetic field
option_c: cancel out the horizontal component of the earth's magnetic field
option_d: cancel out the effects of the magnetic fields found on board the aeroplane
explanation: The purpose of a compass swing is to determine the compass deviation. This is done by measuring the angular difference between Magnetic North and Compass North on various headings, allowing the creation of a correction card.

question_text: In a remote indicating compass system the amount of deviation caused by aircraft magnetism and electrical circuits may be minimised by:
option_a: mounting the detector unit in the wingtip
option_c: positioning the master unit in the centre of the aircraft
explanation: The detector unit of a remote indicating compass contains a flux gate that is sensitive to magnetic fields. Mounting the detector in the wingtip minimizes deviation by keeping it far away from the aircraft's engines, landing gear, and electrical systems.

question_text: A direct reading compass should be swung when:
option_a: there is a large, and permanent, change in magnetic latitude
option_b: there is a large change in magnetic longitude
option_c: the aircraft is stored for a long period and is frequently moved
option_d: the aircraft has made more than a stated number of landings
explanation: A direct-reading compass must be swung after a large and permanent change in magnetic latitude. A change in latitude alters the relative strengths of the horizontal and vertical magnetic components, which changes the aircraft's deviation coefficients.

question_text: The direct reading magnetic compass is made aperiodic (dead beat) by:
option_a: keeping the magnetic assembly mass close to the compass point and by using damping wires
option_b: using the lowest acceptable viscosity compass liquid
option_d: pendulous suspension of the magnetic assembly
explanation: To make a direct-reading compass dead-beat (aperiodic), the magnetic assembly is designed with a low moment of inertia by keeping the mass close to the pivot, and damping wires are immersed in the compass fluid to quickly arrest oscillations.

question_text: The annunciator of a remote indicating compass system is used when:
option_a: synchronising the magnetic and gyro compass elements
explanation: In a remote indicating compass system, the annunciator provides a visual indication of any misalignment between the directional gyroscope and the magnetic flux gate detector, allowing the pilot to manually or automatically synchronize them.

question_text: Which one of the following is an advantage of a remote reading compass as compared with a standby compass?
option_a: It senses the magnetic meridian instead of seeking it, increasing compass sensitivity
option_b: It is lighter than a direct reading compass because it employs, apart from the detector unit, existing aircraft equipment
option_c: It eliminates the effect of turning and acceleration errors by pendulously suspending the detector unit
option_d: It is more reliable because it is operated electrically and power is always available from sources within the aircraft
explanation: A remote reading compass utilizes a flux gate detector that senses the direction of the magnetic field directly without relying on a swinging needle. This increases compass sensitivity and eliminates the friction and inertia issues of standby compasses.

question_text: Which of the following is an occasion for carrying out a compass swing on a Direct Reading Compass?
option_a: After an aircraft has passed through a severe electrical storm, or has been struck by lightning
option_b: Before an aircraft goes on any flight that involves a large change of magnetic latitude
option_c: After any of the aircraft radio equipment has been changed due to unserviceability
option_d: Whenever an aircraft carries a large freight load regardless of its content
explanation: A direct-reading compass swing is required after any event that could alter the aircraft's magnetic signature, such as passing through a severe electrical storm or suffering a lightning strike.

question_text: The main reason for mounting the detector unit of a remote reading compass in the wingtip of an aeroplane is:
option_a: to minimise the amount of deviation caused by aircraft magnetism and electrical circuits
option_b: to maximise the units exposure to the earth's magnetic field
option_c: to ensure that the unit is in the most accessible position on the aircraft for ease of maintenance
option_d: by having detector units on both wingtips, to cancel out the deviation effects caused by the aircraft strucure
explanation: The detector unit (flux gate) of a remote reading compass is placed in the wingtip to maximize its distance from the engines, landing gear, and electrical systems, thereby reducing deviation errors caused by aircraft magnetism.

question_text: The main reason for usually mounting the detector unit of a remote indicating compass in the wingtip of an aeroplane is to:
option_a: reduce the amount of deviation caused by aircraft magnetism and electrical circuits
option_b: facilitate easy maintenance of the unit and increase its exposure to the Earth's magnetic field
option_c: place it in a position where there is no electrical wiring to cause deviation errors
option_d: place it where it will not be subjected to electrical or magnetic interference from the aircraft
explanation: Mounting the magnetic detector unit in the wingtip minimizes compass deviation by positioning the sensor away from the primary sources of electromagnetic interference and ferrous metals inside the aircraft fuselage.

question_text: The main advantage of a remote indicating compass over a direct reading compass is that it:
option_a: senses, rather than seeks, the magnetic meridian
option_d: is able to magnify the earth's magnetic field in order to attain greater accuracy
explanation: Unlike direct-reading standby compasses, a remote indicating compass utilizes a flux gate sensor that electronically measures the direction of the magnetic field directly (sensing it) rather than relying on a card seeking the meridian.

question_text: A chart has the scale 1 : 1 000 000. From A to B on the chart measures 1.5 inches (one inch equals 2.54 centimetres), the distance from A to B in NM is :
explanation: A chart distance of 1.5 inches corresponds to 1.5 * 2.54 = 3.81 cm. At a scale of 1:1,000,000, this represents a ground distance of 3,810,000 cm (38.1 km). Converting to nautical miles: 38.1 / 1.852 = 20.6 NM.

question_text: The nominal scale of a Lambert conformal conic chart is the:
option_b: mean scale between pole and equator
option_c: mean scale between the parallels of the secant cone
explanation: A Lambert conformal conic chart uses a secant cone that intersects the Earth's sphere at two standard parallels. Along these standard parallels, the scale is exactly correct, representing the nominal scale of the chart.

question_text: The chart that is generally used for navigation in polar areas is based on a:
explanation: For navigation in high-latitude polar areas, a Polar Stereographic projection is commonly used because it is conformal, represents meridians as straight lines radiating from the pole, and minimizes distortion in the polar region.

question_text: A Mercator chart has a scale at the equator = 1 : 3 704 000. What is the scale at latitude 60° S?
explanation: On a direct Mercator projection, the scale expands with the secant of the latitude: Scale at Lat = Scale at Equator / cos(Lat). Thus, the scale at 60°S is 1:3,704,000 * cos(60°) = 1:3,704,000 * 0.5 = 1:1,852,000.

question_text: The distance measured between two points on a navigation map is 42 mm (millimetres). The scale of the chart is 1:1 600 000.The actual distance between these two point is approximately:
explanation: A map distance of 42 mm (4.2 cm) on a 1:1,600,000 scale chart represents an Earth distance of 4.2 * 1,600,000 = 6,720,000 cm, which equals 67.2 km. In nautical miles, this is 67.2 / 1.852 = 36.3 NM.

question_text: The standard parallels of a Lambert's conical orthomorphic projection are 07°40'N and 38°20' N.The constant of the cone for this chart is:
explanation: The constant of the cone (n) for a Lambert conformal conic chart is approximately equal to the sine of the parallel of origin (the mean of the standard parallels). For standard parallels at 07°40'N and 38°20'N, n ≈ sin(23°) = 0.39.

question_text: On a Lambert conformal conic chart the convergence of the meridians:
option_a: is the same as earth convergency at the parallel of origin
option_c: varies as the secant of the latitude
option_d: equals earth convergency at the standard parallels
explanation: On a Lambert conformal conic chart, the convergence of the meridians is equal to the constant of the cone (n). Because n represents the sine of the parallel of origin, chart convergence equals Earth convergency at this parallel.

question_text: A straight line drawn on a chart measures 4.63 cm and represents 150 NM. The chart scale is:
explanation: A chart distance of 4.63 cm representing 150 NM (27,780,000 cm) corresponds to a scale ratio of 4.63 / 27,780,000. Simplifying this yields a chart scale of 1:6,000,000.

question_text: On a direct Mercator projection, at latitude 45° North, a certain length represents 70 NM. At latitude 30° North, the same length represents approximately:
explanation: On a direct Mercator chart, the chart distance represented by a given Earth distance varies with the cosine of the latitude. Thus: 70 NM * cos(30°) / cos(45°) = 70 * 0.866 / 0.7071 = 85.7 NM (which is approximately 86 NM).

question_text: On a direct Mercator projection, the distance measured between two meridians spaced 5° apart at latitude 60°N is 8 cm.The scale of this chart at latitude 60°N is approximately:
explanation: At 60°N, the distance along the parallel for 5° dlong is 5 * 60 * cos(60°) = 150 NM. Converting to centimeters: 150 * 185,200 = 27,780,000 cm. A chart distance of 8 cm representing this yields a scale of 8 / 27,780,000 = 1:3,472,500, which is approximately 1:3,500,000.

question_text: On a Mercator chart, the scale:
option_b: varies as the sine of the latitude
option_d: varies as 1/2 cosine of the co-latitude
explanation: On a direct Mercator projection, the scale expands away from the equator as the secant of the latitude, which is mathematically expressed as 1/cosine of the latitude.

question_text: In a navigation chart a distance of 49 NM is equal to 7 cm. The scale of the chart is approximately:
explanation: A distance of 49 NM is equivalent to 49 * 185,200 = 9,074,800 cm. A chart distance of 7 cm representing this length yields a scale ratio of 7 / 9,074,800, which simplifies to approximately 1:1,300,000.

question_text: At 60° N the scale of a direct Mercator chart is 1 : 3 000 000.What is the scale at the equator?
explanation: On a direct Mercator chart, the scale expands away from the equator: Scale at Equator = Scale at Latitude * cos(Latitude). For a scale of 1:3,000,000 at 60°N, the scale at the equator is 1:3,000,000 * cos(60°) = 1:6,000,000.

question_text: What is the chart distance between longitudes 179°E and 175°W on a direct Mercator chart with a scale of 1 : 5 000 000 at the equator?
explanation: The longitude difference between 179°E and 175°W is 6°. Along the equator, this represents an Earth distance of 6 * 60 = 360 NM (66,672,000 cm). At a scale of 1:5,000,000, the chart distance is 66,672,000 / 5,000,000 = 13.33 cm (133 mm).

question_text: The total length of the 53°N parallel of latitude on a direct Mercator chart is 133 cm. What is the approximate scale of the chart at latitude 30°S?
explanation: Given the length of the 53°N parallel on a Mercator chart is 133 cm, the equator length is 133 / cos(53°) = 221 cm. This yields an equatorial scale of 221 / 4,000,000,000 = 1:18,100,000. Applying the latitude expansion factor for 30°S: Scale at 30°S = (1/18,100,000) / cos(30°) ≈ 1:25,000,000.

question_text: A Lambert conformal conic projection, with two standard parallels:
option_a: the scale is only correct along the standard parallels
option_b: shows all great circles as straight lines
option_c: the scale is only correct at parallel of origin
option_d: shows lines of longitude as parallel straight lines
explanation: A Lambert conformal conic projection is created by intersecting the Earth's sphere with a secant cone. The scale is only perfectly correct along the two standard parallels where the cone cuts through the Earth.

question_text: The constant of the cone, on a Lambert chart where the convergence angle between longitudes 010°E and 030°W is 30°, is:
explanation: The constant of the cone (n) is defined as the ratio of chart convergence to the difference in longitude (dlong). For a convergence angle of 30° over a dlong of 40° (10°E to 30°W), n = 30° / 40° = 0.75.

question_text: The constant of cone of a Lambert conformal conic chart is quoted as 0.3955. At what latitude on the chart is earth convergency correctly represented?
explanation: The constant of the cone (n) on a Lambert chart represents the sine of the parallel of origin (latitude of origin). For n = 0.3955, the latitude of origin is arcsin(0.3955) = 23.29° (which is 23°18').

question_text: On a Lambert Conformal chart the distance between meridians 5° apart along latitude 37° North is 9 cm. The scale of the chart at that parallel approximates:
explanation: The Earth distance along the 37°N parallel for a 5° dlong is 5 * 60 * cos(37°) = 239.6 NM (44,374,000 cm). A chart distance of 9 cm representing this length yields a scale ratio of 9 / 44,374,000, which simplifies to approximately 1:5,000,000.

question_text: The chart distance between meridians 10° apart at latitude 65° North is 3.75 inches. The chart scale at this latitude approximates:
explanation: The Earth distance along the 65°N parallel for a 10° dlong is 10 * 60 * cos(65°) = 253.6 NM (46,970,000 cm). A chart distance of 3.75 inches (9.525 cm) yields a scale of 9.525 / 46,970,000, which simplifies to 1:4,930,000 (approximately 1:5,000,000).

question_text: On a Lambert conformal conic chart, with two standard parallels, the quoted scale is correct:
option_b: in the area between the standard parallels
explanation: On a Lambert conformal conic projection using two standard parallels, the scale factor is exactly 1.0 (correct scale) only along those two standard parallels.

question_text: The convergence factor of a Lambert conformal conic chart is quoted as 0.78535. At what latitude on the chart is earth convergency correctly represented?
explanation: The convergence factor (n) of a Lambert conformal conic chart equals the sine of the latitude of origin. For n = 0.78535, the latitude at which chart convergence matches Earth convergency is arcsin(0.78535) = 51.75° (which is 51°45').

question_text: At 47° North the chart distance between meridians 10° apart is 5 inches. The scale of the chart at 47° North approximates:
explanation: The Earth distance along the 47°N parallel for a 10° dlong is 10 * 60 * cos(47°) = 409.2 NM (75,784,000 cm). A chart distance of 5 inches (12.7 cm) yields a scale of 12.7 / 75,784,000, which simplifies to approximately 1:6,000,000.

question_text: On a Lambert Conformal Conic chart earth convergency is most accurately represented at the:
option_b: north and south limits of the chart
explanation: A Lambert conformal conic chart represents Earth convergency exactly at the parallel of origin, where the constant of the cone (n) equals the sine of the latitude.

question_text: On a Transverse Mercator chart, scale is exactly correct along the:
option_b: Equator, parallel of origin and prime vertical
option_c: datum meridian and meridian perpendicular to it
explanation: A Transverse Mercator projection uses a cylinder that is tangent to the Earth along a chosen central meridian. The scale is perfectly correct (scale factor of 1.0) along this central meridian of tangency.

question_text: Approximately how many nautical miles correspond to 12 cm on a map with a scale of 1 : 2 000 000?
explanation: A map distance of 12 cm at a scale of 1:2,000,000 represents an Earth distance of 12 * 2,000,000 = 24,000,000 cm (240 km). Converting to nautical miles: 240 / 1.852 = 129.6 NM, which rounds to 130 NM.

question_text: Transverse Mercator projections are used for:
option_b: maps of large east/west extent in equatorial areas
option_c: radio navigation charts in equatorial areas
explanation: Because the cylinder of a Transverse Mercator projection is tangent along a central meridian, distortion is minimized along a north-south line. This projection is therefore ideal for mapping areas of large north-south extent.

question_text: On a Direct Mercator chart at latitude 15°S, a certain length represents a distance of 120 NM on the earth. The same length on the chart will represent on the earth, at latitude 10°N, a distance of :
explanation: On a direct Mercator chart, the en-route distance represented by a given chart length varies as the cosine of the latitude. Therefore, the distance represented at 10°N is 120 NM * cos(10°) / cos(15°) = 120 * 0.9848 / 0.9659 = 122.3 NM.

question_text: On a Direct Mercator chart at latitude of 45°N, a certain length represents a distance of 90 NM on the earth. The same length on the chart will represent on the earth, at latitude 30°N, a distance of :
explanation: On a direct Mercator chart, the en-route distance represented by a given chart length is proportional to the cosine of the latitude. Thus, the distance represented at 30°N is 90 NM * cos(30°) / cos(45°) = 90 * 0.8660 / 0.7071 = 110 NM.

question_text: On a transverse Mercator chart, the scale is exactly correct along the:
option_c: meridian of tangency and the parallel of latitude perpendicular to it
explanation: A Transverse Mercator projection is constructed with a cylinder tangent to the Earth along a central meridian. The scale is exact (scale factor of 1.0) along this central meridian of tangency.

question_text: On a transverse Mercator chart, with the exception of the Equator, parallels of latitude appear as:
explanation: On a Transverse Mercator projection, parallels of latitude are projected as curves that form ellipses on the flat map surface, with the exception of the equator which is a straight line.

question_text: An Oblique Mercator projection is used specifically to produce:
option_a: charts of the great circle route between two points
option_b: radio navigational charts in equatorial regions
option_c: topographical maps of large east/ west extent
explanation: An Oblique Mercator projection uses a cylinder that is tangent to the Earth along a chosen great circle. This alignment makes it ideal for producing strip maps of the great circle route between two specific locations.

question_text: The two standard parallels of a conical Lambert projection are at N10°40'N and N41°20'.The cone constant of this chart is approximatively :
explanation: The constant of the cone (n) is approximately equal to the sine of the parallel of origin (mean latitude). For standard parallels at 10°40'N and 41°20'N (mean latitude 26°), n ≈ sin(26°) = 0.44.

question_text: On a chart, the distance along a meridian between latitudes 45°N and 46°N is 6 cm. The scale of the chart is approximately:
explanation: The distance along a meridian for 1° of latitude is 60 NM (11,112,000 cm). A chart distance of 6 cm representing 1° of latitude yields a scale ratio of 6 / 11,112,000, which simplifies to approximately 1:1,850,000.

question_text: Given:Chart scale is 1 : 1 850 000. The chart distance between two points is 4 centimetres. Earth distance is approximately :
explanation: At a scale of 1:1,850,000, a chart distance of 4 cm represents an Earth distance of 4 * 1,850,000 = 7,400,000 cm (74 km). Converting to nautical miles: 74 / 1.852 = 39.95 NM (approximately 40 NM).

question_text: On a Mercator chart, at latitude 60°N, the distance measured between W002° and E008° is 20 cm. The scale of this chart at latitude 60°N is approximately:
explanation: The distance along the 60°N parallel for a 10° dlong (W002° to E008°) is 10 * 60 * cos(60°) = 300 NM (55,560,000 cm). A chart distance of 20 cm yields a scale at 60°N of 20 / 55,560,000, which simplifies to approximately 1:2,780,000.

question_text: At latitude 60°N the scale of a Mercator projection is 1 : 5 000 000. The length on the chart between 'C' N60° E008° and 'D' N60° W008° is:
explanation: The distance along the 60°N parallel for a 16° dlong (E008° to W008°) is 16 * 60 * cos(60°) = 480 NM (88,896,000 cm). At a scale of 1:5,000,000, the chart length is 88,896,000 / 5,000,000 = 17.78 cm (approximately 17.8 cm).

question_text: Assume a Mercator chart.The distance between positions A and B, located on the same parallel and 10° longitude apart, is 6 cm. The scale at the parallel is 1 : 9 260 000.What is the latitude of A and B?
explanation: Distance = 10° * 60 * cos(lat) NM. Convert to cm: Distance = 600 * cos(lat) * 1.852 * 100,000 = 111,120,000 * cos(lat) cm. Chart distance = Distance / Scale => 6 = 111,120,000 * cos(lat) / 9,260,000 => 6 = 12 * cos(lat) => cos(lat) = 0.5, which gives a latitude of 60° N or S.

question_text: A straight line on a chart 4.89 cm long represents 185 NM.The scale of this chart is approximately :
explanation: A distance of 185 NM is equivalent to 185 * 1.852 * 100,000 = 34,262,000 cm. A chart distance of 4.89 cm representing this length yields a scale ratio of 4.89 / 34,262,000, which simplifies to approximately 1:7,000,000.

question_text: The scale on a Lambert conformal conic chart :
option_a: is constant along a parallel of latitude
option_b: is constant along a meridian of longitude
option_c: is constant across the whole map
option_d: varies slightly as a function of latitude and longitude
explanation: On a Lambert conformal conic chart, scale varies with latitude but is uniform along any single parallel. Therefore, the chart scale remains constant along any given parallel of latitude.

question_text: A direct Mercator graticule is based on a projection that is :
explanation: A direct Mercator projection is a conformal cylindrical projection where the cylinder is tangent to the Earth's surface along the equator.

question_text: Parallels of latitude on a Direct Mercator chart are :
option_c: arcs of concentric circles equally spaced
option_d: straight lines converging above the pole
explanation: On a direct Mercator chart, parallels of latitude are projected as parallel straight lines that are unequally spaced, with the spacing increasing towards the poles to maintain conformality.

question_text: A straight line on a Lambert Conformal Projection chart for normal flight planning purposes:
option_d: can only be a parallel of latitude
explanation: For standard flight planning over mid-latitudes, a straight line drawn on a Lambert conformal conic chart is a very close approximation of a Great Circle track.

question_text: On a Direct Mercator chart, a rhumb line appears as a:
option_b: small circle concave to the nearer pole
option_d: curve convex to the nearer pole
explanation: On a direct Mercator chart, meridians and parallels are straight lines that intersect at 90°. Consequently, a line of constant course (a rhumb line) appears as a simple straight line.

question_text: On a Lambert Conformal Conic chart great circles that are not meridians are:
option_a: curves concave to the parallel of origin
option_c: curves concave to the pole of projection
option_d: straight lines within the standard parallels
explanation: On a Lambert conformal conic chart, parallels of latitude are projected as concentric circles. Great circles (other than meridians) are projected as curves that are concave towards the parallel of origin (or the pole of projection).

question_text: On a Direct Mercator chart a great circle will be represented by a:
explanation: On a direct Mercator chart, a great circle track (which curves toward the poles) is represented as a curve that is concave towards the equator.

question_text: The angular difference, on a Lambert conformal conic chart, between the arrival and departure track is equal to:
explanation: Map convergence represents the angular difference between the meridians at the departure and arrival points on a Lambert conformal conic chart, which is also the difference between the track angles of a straight line at those points.

question_text: The parallels on a Lambert Conformal Conic chart are represented by:
explanation: Parallels of latitude on a Lambert conformal conic chart are projected as arcs of concentric circles centered at the apex of the cone.

question_text: Parallels of latitude, except the equator, are:
option_c: both Rhumb lines and Great circles
option_d: are neither Rhumb lines nor Great circles
explanation: All parallels of latitude cross all meridians of longitude at a constant angle of 90°, making them rhumb lines. Only the equator is also a great circle.

question_text: On a Lambert chart (standard parallels 37°N and 65°N), with respect to the straight line drawn on the map between A ( N49° W030°) and B (N48° W040°), the:
option_a: great circle and rhumb line are to the south
option_b: great circle and rhumb line are to the north
option_c: great circle is to the north, the rhumb line is to the south
option_d: rhumb line is to the north, the great circle is to the south
explanation: A straight line on a Lambert conformal conic chart is a very close approximation of a great circle. Since the parallel of origin is north of the flight path, the straight line lies north of the actual great circle track. Thus, both the actual great circle path on the Earth and the rhumb line lie to the south of the straight line drawn on the chart.

question_text: On a Direct Mercator chart, meridians are:
option_a: parallel, equally spaced, vertical straight lines
option_b: inclined, equally spaced, straight lines that meet at the nearer pole
option_c: parallel, unequally spaced, vertical straight lines
option_d: inclined, unequally spaced, curved lines that meet at the nearer pole
explanation: On a Direct Mercator chart, meridians of longitude are projected as parallel, equally spaced, vertical straight lines that intersect parallels of latitude at right angles.

question_text: On which of the following chart projections is it NOT possible to represent the north or south poles?
explanation: On a Direct Mercator projection, the spacing of latitude parallels increases as the secant of the latitude, which becomes infinite at 90° (the poles), making it mathematically impossible to project the poles.

question_text: Which one of the following, concerning great circles on a Direct Mercator chart, is correct?
option_a: With the exception of meridians and the equator, they are curves concave to the equator
option_b: They are all curves concave to the equator
option_c: They approximate to straight lines between the standard parallels
option_d: They are all curves convex to the equator
explanation: Since great circles curve towards the poles relative to rhumb lines, they are represented on a Direct Mercator projection as curves that are concave towards the equator (or convex towards the nearest pole).

question_text: On a Lambert conformal conic chart, the distance between parallels of latitude spaced the same number of degrees apart :
option_a: reduces between, and expands outside, the standard parallels
option_b: is constant between, and expands outside, the standard parallels
option_c: expands between, and reduces outside, the standard parallels
explanation: Due to the secant cone projection, the scale factor on a Lambert conformal conic chart is less than 1.0 (compressed) between the standard parallels and greater than 1.0 (expanded) outside of them.

question_text: Which one of the following statements is correct concerning the appearance of great circles, with the exception of meridians, on a Polar Stereographic chart whose tangency is at the pole ?
option_a: The higher the latitude the closer they approximate to a straight line
option_b: Any straight line is a great circle
option_c: They are complex curves that can be convex and/or concave to the Pole
option_d: They are curves convex to the Pole
explanation: On a Polar Stereographic chart, great circles are projected as curves that are concave towards the pole. As latitude increases towards the pole of tangency, the curvature decreases, and the path closely approximates a straight line.

question_text: Which one of the following describes the appearance of rhumb lines, except meridians, on a Polar Stereographic chart?
explanation: On a Polar Stereographic projection, rhumb lines are represented as spiral-like curves that are concave towards the pole.

question_text: What is the value of the convergence factor on a Polar Stereographic chart?
explanation: On a Polar Stereographic chart, the parallel of origin is the pole itself (90° latitude), meaning the constant of the cone (convergence factor) is n = sin(90°) = 1.0.

question_text: On a Direct Mercator, rhumb lines are:
explanation: Because meridians and parallels are straight lines intersecting at 90° on a Direct Mercator projection, a line of constant track angle (a rhumb line) is represented as a straight line.

question_text: Contour lines on aeronautical maps and charts connect points :
option_a: having the same elevation above sea level
explanation: Contour lines are isolines drawn on charts to connect points of equal elevation above a specified vertical datum, typically mean sea level.

question_text: On a Polar Stereographic chart, the initial great circle course from A 70°N 060°W to B 70°N 060°E is approximately:
explanation: On a Polar Stereographic chart, the meridians converge at the pole with a convergence factor of 1.0. The path is a straight line between A and B, crossing the meridian at the midpoint (0° longitude) at 90°(T). The convergence angle is dlong * 1.0 = 120°. The initial track at A is 90° - (120° / 2) = 030°(T).

question_text: On a polar stereographic projection chart showing the South Pole, a straight line joins position A (70°S 065°E) to position B (70°S 025°W).The true course on departure from position A is approximately:
explanation: Over the Southern Hemisphere, a straight line on a Polar Stereographic chart has a track angle that changes with the convergence of meridians. With a dlong of 90° (065°E to 025°W) and n = 1.0, the track changes by 90°. In the Southern Hemisphere, the departure track is 270° - (90° / 2) = 225°.

question_text: Two positions plotted on a polar stereographic chart, A (80°N 000°) and B (70°N 102°W) are joined by a straight line whose highest latitude is reached at 035°W.At point B, the true course is:
explanation: The highest latitude on the straight line represents the vertex, where the track crosses the meridian of 35°W at exactly 270°(T) going west. The difference in longitude from the vertex to B is 102° - 35° = 67°. Since n = 1.0, the track angle changes by 67°, resulting in a track at B of 270° - 67° = 203°(T).

question_text: Given:Magnetic heading 311°Drift angle 10° leftRelative bearing of NDB 270°What is the magnetic bearing of the NDB measured from the aircraft?
explanation: The magnetic bearing of the NDB is calculated by adding the relative bearing of the station to the magnetic heading of the aircraft: 311° + 270° = 581°. Subtracting 360° yields 221° magnetic bearing.

question_text: A Lambert conformal conic chart has a constant of the cone of 0.75. The initial course of a straight line track drawn on this chart from A (40°N 050°W) to B is 043°(T) at A, course at B is 055°(T). What is the longitude of B?
explanation: The change in course along a straight line track on a Lambert chart equals the chart convergence: Change = 55° - 43° = 12°. Since chart convergence = dlong * constant of the cone, dlong = 12° / 0.75 = 16° E. Therefore, the longitude of B is 50°W - 16° = 34°W.

question_text: A Lambert conformal conic chart has a constant of the cone of 0.80. A straight line course drawn on this chart from A (53°N 004°W) to B is 080° at A, course at B is 092°(T). What is the longitude of B?
explanation: The track change along the straight line equals the chart convergence: 92° - 80° = 12°. With a constant of the cone of 0.80, the difference in longitude is dlong = 12° / 0.80 = 15° E. The longitude of B is 4°W - 15° = 11°E.

question_text: Given the following:True track: 192°Magnetic variation: 7°EDrift angle: 5° leftWhat is the magnetic heading required to maintain the given track?
explanation: Magnetic variation is 7°E, so the required magnetic track is 192° - 7° = 185°(M). With a drift of 5° left, the aircraft must head 5° to the right to counteract the drift: 185° + 5° = 190° magnetic heading.

question_text: Given the following:Magnetic heading: 060°Magnetic variation: 8°WDrift angle: 4° rightWhat is the true track?
explanation: True heading is magnetic heading minus westerly variation: 060° - 8° = 052°(T). With a drift angle of 4° right, the true track is true heading plus drift: 052° + 4° = 056°(T).

question_text: Given: True track 180°Drift 8°RCompass heading 195°Deviation -2°Calculate the variation?
explanation: True heading is true track minus right drift: 180° - 8° = 172°(T). Magnetic heading is compass heading plus deviation: 195° + (-2°) = 193°(M). Variation is true heading minus magnetic heading: 172° - 193° = -21°, which corresponds to 21°W.

question_text: Given: True course 300°drift 8°Rvariation 10°Wdeviation -4° Calculate the compass heading?
explanation: True heading is true course minus right drift: 300° - 8° = 292°(T). Magnetic heading is true heading plus westerly variation: 292° + 10° = 302°(M). Compass heading is magnetic heading minus westerly deviation: 302° - (-4°) = 306°(C).

question_text: Given:true track 352°variation 11° Wdeviation is -5°drift 10°R.Calculate the compass heading?

question_text: Given:true track 070°variation 30°Wdeviation +1°drift 10°RCalculate the compass heading?

question_text: Given: True course from A to B = 090°,TAS = 460 kt, W/V = 360/100kt,Average variation = 10°E,Deviation = -2°.Calculate the compass heading and GS?
explanation: Solving the wind triangle (track 090°, TAS 460 kt, wind 360°/100 kt) yields a wind correction angle (WCA) of 12.5° left, meaning True Heading is 077.5°(T), and Groundspeed is 449 kt. Magnetic heading is 077.5° - 10°E = 067.5°(M), and Compass Heading is 067.5° - (-2°) = 069.5°(C), which matches option A (069° - 448 kt).

question_text: How many NM would an aircraft travel in 1 MIN 45 SEC if GS is 135 kt?
explanation: 1 minute 45 seconds is 1.75 minutes. The distance traveled is Groundspeed * (time in minutes / 60) = 135 * (1.75 / 60) = 3.9375 NM, which rounds to 3.94 NM.

question_text: Fuel flow per HR is 22 US-GAL, total fuel on board is 83 IMP GAL.What is the endurance?
explanation: Converting Imperial Gallons to US Gallons: 83 IMP GAL * 1.20095 = 99.68 US GAL. Endurance is 99.68 / 22 = 4.53 hours, which equals 4 hours and 32 minutes.

question_text: What is the ratio between the litre and the US-GAL ?
explanation: By standard international volume conversions, 1 US Gallon is defined as exactly 3.78541 liters.

question_text: 265 US-GAL equals? (Specific gravity 0.80)
explanation: First, convert US Gallons to liters: 265 US GAL * 3.7854 = 1003.1 liters. Mass in kilograms is volume in liters multiplied by specific gravity: 1003.1 * 0.80 = 802.5 kg, which is approximately 803 kg.

question_text: 730 FT/MIN equals:
explanation: Converting feet per minute to meters per second: 1 foot = 0.3048 meters, and 1 minute = 60 seconds. So 730 * (0.3048 / 60) = 3.71 m/s (approx 3.7 m/sec).

question_text: How long will it take to fly 5 NM at a groundspeed of 269 Kt ?
explanation: Time = 5 / 269 = 0.018587 hours. In seconds, this is 0.018587 * 3600 = 66.9 seconds, which corresponds to 1 minute and 7 seconds.

question_text: An aircraft travels 2.4 statute miles in 47 seconds. What is its groundspeed?
explanation: The speed is 2.4 statute miles / 47 seconds = 0.05106 SM/sec = 183.8 SM/hr. Converting to knots: 183.8 / 1.15078 = 159.7 kt, which rounds to 160 kt.

question_text: An aircraft travels 100 statute miles in 20 MIN, how long does it take to travel 215 NM?
explanation: Speed is 100 SM / 20 min = 5 SM/min = 300 SM/hr. Converting to knots: 300 / 1.1508 = 260.7 kt. The time to travel 215 NM is 215 / 260.7 = 0.825 hours = 49.5 minutes, which rounds to 50 minutes.

question_text: The equivalent of 70 m/sec is approximately:
explanation: Converting meters per second to knots: 70 m/s * (3600 sec/hr) / (1852 meters/NM) = 136.06 kt.

question_text: Given:FL 350,Mach 0.80,OAT -55°C. Calculate the values for TAS and local speed of sound (LSS)?

question_text: Given: Pressure Altitude 29000 FT, OAT -55°C. Calculate the Density Altitude?

question_text: Given:TAS = 485 kt,OAT = ISA +10°C,FL 410.Calculate the Mach Number?

question_text: What is the ISA temperature value at FL 330?

question_text: Given: FL250, OAT -15 ºC, TAS 250 kt.Calculate the Mach No.?
